authoritative_sources.title: Family-Centred Maternity and Newborn Care: National Guidelines — Chapter 5: Postpartum Care
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Official PHAC page dated 2024-08-01; it is the current national Chapter 5 and supersedes the earlier postpartum chapter edition.

supported_recommendations.statement: In a patient from birth through 6 weeks postpartum, fever or chills with lower abdominal pain, uterine tenderness, tachycardia, or foul-smelling/bloody discharge supports postpartum endometritis and requires prompt clinical assessment and antibiotic treatment.

The postpartum fever differential should be localized by accompanying findings: uterine/lochia findings suggest endometritis or urinary infection, whereas a red, hot, painful breast with systemic symptoms suggests mastitis.

source_citations.locator: Section 3.2 Care of the Mother, Signs and symptoms of concern; Section 4.3 Infections

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Postpartum endometritis can occur at any time from birth through 6 weeks postpartum; a later presentation is not excluded solely by timing.

source_family_target_assessments.rationale: The 2024 PHAC national postpartum guideline directly covers postpartum fever and infection; no current SOGC document with equivalent postpartum-fever diagnostic scope was found.

evidence_boundaries.statement: Fever alone is nonspecific; uterine tenderness and abnormal lochia support endometritis, while focal breast findings support mastitis. Hemodynamic instability or heavy bleeding requires emergency assessment rather than routine outpatient follow-up.

source_citations.locator: Signs and symptoms of concern; Sections 4.2–4.3

evidence_notes: Evidence extraction is restricted to postpartum infection recognition and urgent diagnostic boundaries required by SU-OB-53.

authoritative_sources.title: Family-Centred Maternity and Newborn Care: National Guidelines — Chapter 6: Breastfeeding
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Official PHAC Chapter 6 page shows page date 2023-10-25; Open Government metadata records original publication 2018-06-20. No newer PHAC breastfeeding chapter was identified.

supported_recommendations.statement: Lactational mastitis is suggested by localized breast tenderness, redness, and heat with systemic fever or malaise; diffuse bilateral engorgement in an otherwise well patient is a different pattern.

source_citations.locator: Section 5, Mastitis; comparison table for engorgement, plugged ducts, and mastitis

supported_recommendations.statement: A tender mass that persists as mastitis symptoms improve, particularly when fluctuant, raises concern for breast abscess and should prompt ultrasound-guided aspiration or surgical assessment if aspiration fails.
Breastfeeding should generally continue during mastitis; milk remains safe for the infant even when maternal antibiotics are required.

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Recurrence in the same breast location warrants evaluation for an underlying mass or other abnormality rather than repeated presumptive treatment alone.

source_family_target_assessments.rationale: PHAC's national postpartum and breastfeeding chapters directly cover mastitis, abscess, and breastfeeding continuation; no current SOGC mastitis guideline with equivalent scope was found.

evidence_boundaries.statement: Localized inflammatory findings plus systemic illness support mastitis; a persistent fluctuant mass supports abscess; diffuse engorgement without systemic illness should not be labelled mastitis.

source_citations.locator: Section 5, comparison of engorgement, plugged ducts, mastitis, and abscess

evidence_notes: No antibiotic regimen was added because the canonical evidence requirement is DIAGNOSIS; the management boundary is limited to continuing breastfeeding and recognizing abscess.

authoritative_sources.title: Family-Centred Maternity and Newborn Care: National Guidelines — Chapter 5: Postpartum Care
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Official PHAC page dated 2024-08-01; current national postpartum chapter.

authoritative_sources.title: Family-Centred Maternity and Newborn Care: National Guidelines — Chapter 6: Breastfeeding
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Official PHAC Chapter 6 page shows page date 2023-10-25; Open Government metadata records original publication 2018-06-20. No newer PHAC chapter was identified.

supported_recommendations.statement: Routine postpartum care should be individualized, include maternal and infant assessment, an established discharge and follow-up plan, and follow-up of the mother within 48 hours after discharge.

source_citations.locator: Section 3 Early Postpartum Care, personalized care plan and follow-up

supported_recommendations.statement: Breastfeeding medication safety should be assessed for the specific drug and clinical context; most maternal illnesses are compatible with breastfeeding, but some therapies such as radioisotopes or chemotherapy may be incompatible.

source_citations.locator: Contraindications to Breastfeeding and Temporary Interruptions

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Breastfeeding is not universally safe in every circumstance: classic galactosemia in the infant, active untreated maternal tuberculosis, and incompatible maternal therapies require replacement feeding or interruption according to the specific condition.

source_family_target_assessments.rationale: PHAC national chapters provide the current routine postpartum and breastfeeding medication-safety framework; no single current SOGC guideline covers this combined canonical requirement.

evidence_boundaries.statement: Do not advise stopping breastfeeding merely because a medication is prescribed; assess the particular drug. Conversely, do not assume all medications or procedures are compatible.

evidence_notes: The packet records general postpartum follow-up and medication-safety boundaries, not drug-specific prescribing claims outside its canonical DIAGNOSIS requirement.

authoritative_sources.title: Immunization in pregnancy and breastfeeding: Canadian Immunization Guide
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Public Health Agency of Canada / National Advisory Committee on Immunization
authoritative_sources.guideline_version: Canadian Immunization Guide Part 3; partial update August 2026
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Evergreen Canadian Immunization Guide chapter, last partial update August 2026 and last complete revision April 2018. The page lists several pending incorporations, none material to the routine influenza, Tdap, or pregnancy live-vaccine claims extracted here.

authoritative_sources.title: SOGC Statement on RSV Immunization to Prevent Infant RSV Infection
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Still listed by SOGC among current position statements. Its RSV timing predates NACI's April/August 2026 update and is interpreted in that newer national context.

guideline_versions: Canadian Immunization Guide Part 3; partial update August 2026

supported_recommendations.statement: Offer non-live influenza vaccine during every pregnancy at any gestational stage and Tdap during every pregnancy regardless of prior Tdap history, ideally at 27–32 weeks; earlier 13–26 week administration may be considered when preterm delivery risk is increased, and missed Tdap can be given up to delivery.

source_citations.locator: Recommended vaccines — Non-live influenza and Pertussis; Table 1

supported_recommendations.statement: Live vaccines are generally contraindicated during pregnancy; preconception live vaccination should be followed by avoiding pregnancy for at least 28 days, while inadvertent MMR or varicella vaccination is not by itself an indication for pregnancy termination.

For infant RSV prevention, use the current national program context: maternal RSVpreF may be considered at 28–36 weeks in advance of or during RSV season and is generally unnecessary when the infant will receive nirsevimab or clesrovimab.

source_citations.locator: Table 1 — Respiratory syncytial virus vaccine; Chapter revision process

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Some live vaccines may be considered only when the exposure risk clearly outweighs the theoretical fetal risk; inadvertent administration of MMR or varicella vaccine is not a reason for pregnancy termination.

evidence_boundaries.statement: Do not defer indicated non-live influenza vaccine because of trimester, and do not omit Tdap because a dose was given before the current pregnancy. Do not routinely give live attenuated vaccines during pregnancy.

The 2024 SOGC maternal RSV window of 32+0–36+6 weeks is narrower than the updated 2026 national 28–36 week window; use the newer NACI/Canadian Immunization Guide recommendation for current MCCQE-context questions.

evidence_notes: The Canadian Immunization Guide was checked for its August 2026 update and for notices of recommendations not yet incorporated; the extracted routine pregnancy recommendations are not affected by those notices.

disagreements_or_ambiguities.summary: SOGC's July 2024 statement offers maternal RSVpreF at 32+0–36+6 weeks when infant nirsevimab is unavailable or declined; the August 2026 Canadian Immunization Guide reflects newer NACI guidance allowing 28–36 weeks and includes nirsevimab or clesrovimab as infant alternatives.
disagreements_or_ambiguities.canadian_mccqe_applicability: Use the newer NACI/PHAC national recommendation for current Canadian MCCQE content; retain the SOGC statement as dated specialty context.

authoritative_sources.title: Guideline No. 461: The Management of Uterine Fibroids
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Published August 2025 after literature review through January 2025; explicitly replaces SOGC Guideline No. 318. No superseding SOGC fibroid guideline was found.

authoritative_sources.title: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding: Care for Adults and Adolescents of Reproductive Age
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Ontario Health published the evidence-updated standard in August 2024; the official standard page remained published and was last updated 2026-06-26.

supported_recommendations.statement: Use ultrasound as first-line imaging when uterine structural pathology such as fibroids is suspected; MRI is reserved for complex cases or surgical planning rather than routine first-line use.

Perform endometrial biopsy for heavy menstrual bleeding when endometrial cancer or hyperplasia risk factors are present; biopsy samples endometrial cells but does not reliably identify focal endometrial lesions.

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Transabdominal pelvic ultrasound alone may be more appropriate when transvaginal imaging is not suitable; further evaluation may use saline-infusion sonography, hysteroscopy, or MRI according to the suspected lesion.

evidence_boundaries.statement: Imaging is not a substitute for endometrial sampling when cancer or hyperplasia risk is present, and blind endometrial biopsy is not a reliable test for a focal cavity lesion.

evidence_notes: This packet is limited to generalist selection of pelvic imaging and endometrial biopsy; it does not encode specialist procedural technique.

authoritative_sources.title: No. 377—Hysterectomy for Benign Gynaecologic Indications
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: This guideline superseded SOGC No. 109. Its stated five-year review point has passed, but no replacement or retirement was found; Ontario Health's 2024 standard remains concordant with its core recommendations.

authoritative_sources.title: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding: Care for Adults and Adolescents of Reproductive Age
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Published August 2024 after evidence review; official standard page remained published and was last updated 2026-06-26.

supported_recommendations.statement: For benign heavy menstrual bleeding, offer hysterectomy only after documented discussion of less invasive medical and surgical alternatives or after other treatments have failed, incorporating the patient's goals and preferences.

When hysterectomy for a benign indication is chosen, vaginal or laparoscopic routes are preferred where feasible; counsel about perioperative risks, ovarian conservation/removal implications, and urinary tract injury.

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Correct preoperative anemia when elective hysterectomy is planned; SOGC identifies hemoglobin below 120 g/L as requiring correction to reduce perioperative morbidity and mortality.

evidence_boundaries.statement: Hysterectomy is definitive but not the automatic first treatment for benign heavy bleeding; offer medication and less invasive procedures first unless clinical circumstances require otherwise.

evidence_notes: Operative technique details were excluded; the packet supports generalist counselling, indication, complication, and referral decisions.

authoritative_sources.title: Current evaluation of amenorrhea: a committee opinion (2024)
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: American Society for Reproductive Medicine Practice Committee
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: ASRM's 2024 committee opinion explicitly replaces its 2008 document. No current Canadian national or SOGC general amenorrhea-evaluation guideline was found.

supported_recommendations.statement: Exclude pregnancy first in secondary amenorrhea. Primary amenorrhea requires evaluation by age 15 with normal secondary sexual development, within 5 years of breast development when it begins before age 10, or when breast development has not begun by age 13; secondary amenorrhea requires investigation after more than 3 months with previously regular cycles or 6 months with irregular cycles.

After pregnancy is excluded, use history, examination, prolactin, TSH, FSH and estradiol to distinguish hypothalamic/pituitary, ovarian, and outflow-tract or uterine causes; pelvic ultrasound can streamline evaluation when accessible.

source_citations.locator: Evaluation of the Patient; Secondary Amenorrhea — Laboratory tests and Pelvic ultrasound

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Rapidly progressive virilization requires exclusion of an androgen-secreting ovarian or adrenal tumour rather than routine attribution to polycystic ovary syndrome.

source_citations.locator: Secondary Amenorrhea — History and Physical examination

source_family_target_assessments.rationale: No current Canadian national or SOGC guideline covering the complete primary/secondary amenorrhea evaluation was found; ASRM's current specialty committee opinion directly matches the canonical requirement.

evidence_boundaries.statement: Do not diagnose PCOS before excluding pregnancy and other endocrine or structural causes; the progesterone-withdrawal test can be misleading and must be interpreted in clinical and ultrasound context.

source_citations.locator: Secondary Amenorrhea — Pregnancy test, Laboratory tests, and Progesterone withdrawal test

evidence_notes: CANADIAN_GUIDANCE_NOT_FOUND = true. Canadian PCOS pathways were not used as a substitute for a complete amenorrhea differential because they cover only one etiologic compartment.

international_fallbacks.reason: No current Canadian national or SOGC guideline was found that covers the complete primary and secondary amenorrhea evaluation required by this packet.

source_citations.locator: Introduction; Evaluation; Primary and Secondary Amenorrhea sections

authoritative_sources.title: No. 292—Abnormal Uterine Bleeding in Pre-Menopausal Women
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Reaffirmed by SOGC in 2018. No replacement general AUB guideline was found; Ontario Health's 2024 evidence update cites this SOGC guidance and supplies current care standards.

authoritative_sources.title: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding: Care for Adults and Adolescents of Reproductive Age
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Published August 2024 after evidence review; official standard page remained published and was last updated 2026-06-26.

supported_recommendations.statement: Evaluate reproductive-age abnormal uterine bleeding systematically: characterize bleeding, exclude pregnancy when possible, assess anemia, and use the PALM-COEIN framework to consider structural and non-structural causes before selecting treatment.

For stable heavy menstrual bleeding, offer shared choice among non-hormonal options such as tranexamic acid or NSAIDs and hormonal options such as an LNG intrauterine system, combined hormonal contraception, or continuous progestin, matched to contraindications and patient goals.
Acute uncontrolled heavy bleeding requires prompt stabilization and bleeding control, rapid treatment of severe anemia, and follow-up at or immediately after the next period, approximately 4 weeks.

source_citations.locator: Quality Statement 8: Acute Heavy Menstrual Bleeding, pages 23–24

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Endometrial biopsy is indicated when endometrial cancer or hyperplasia risk factors are present, including age over 40, chronic anovulation, persistent intermenstrual bleeding, obesity, diabetes, or prolonged unopposed estrogen exposure.

evidence_boundaries.statement: Dilation and curettage is not routine investigation or treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding; reserve it for acute uncontrolled bleeding when medical therapy is ineffective or contraindicated.

evidence_notes: Ontario's standard excludes pregnancy, postmenopause, and bleeding within 3 months of delivery, miscarriage, or abortion; those scenarios require their own pathways.

authoritative_sources.title: Guideline No. 329 — Canadian Contraception Consensus, Parts 1–4
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: The component chapters were published from October 2015 through April 2017 and remain linked in SOGC's active Guideline 329 resource kit. No superseding Canadian Contraception Consensus was found; newer method-specific SOGC position statements do not replace the suite.

supported_recommendations.statement: Select contraception through patient-centred counselling that weighs effectiveness, medical conditions and contraindications, concurrent medications, side effects, non-contraceptive benefits, access, and the patient's preferences.

Provide emergency contraception as soon as possible after unprotected intercourse. The copper IUD is the most effective option; ulipristal is more effective than levonorgestrel through 5 days, particularly after 72 hours, while levonorgestrel effectiveness declines with delay.

source_citations.locator: Chapter 3 Emergency Contraception, Summary Statements 12–18 and Recommendations 16–18

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: After ulipristal emergency contraception, delay initiation of hormonal contraception for 5 days and use backup contraception; levonorgestrel emergency contraception permits immediate or next-day hormonal initiation with backup.

source_citations.locator: Chapter 3 Emergency Contraception, Summary Statements 19–20 and Recommendations 19–20

evidence_boundaries.statement: Do not choose a contraceptive solely by theoretical efficacy or assume all hormonal methods share the same contraindications; method selection is individualized. For emergency contraception, do not delay care while waiting for the next menstrual period.

evidence_notes: The active SOGC resource kit was checked for supersession. Claims are confined to methods and emergency-contraception recommendations covered by Guideline 329.

source_citations.locator: Guideline No. 329, Parts 1–4 and active SOGC resource kit

authoritative_sources.title: Guideline No. 461: The Management of Uterine Fibroids
authoritative_sources.issuing_organization: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada
authoritative_sources.currentness_notes: Published August 2025 after literature review through January 2025; explicitly replaces SOGC Guideline No. 318.

supported_recommendations.statement: Manage fibroids according to symptoms, age, preferences, fertility goals, and fibroid number, size, and location. Asymptomatic fibroids generally require no treatment; symptomatic bleeding or bulk symptoms warrant investigation and individualized therapy.

Medical options for fibroid-related bleeding include oral contraceptives, progestins including an LNG intrauterine system, GnRH agonists or antagonists, danazol, and tranexamic acid. Hysterectomy is definitive; myomectomy may preserve fertility or the uterus, and uterine artery embolization may preserve the uterus but is not advised when future fertility is desired.

important_contraindications_or_exception.statement: Do not recommend hysterectomy solely to prevent malignancy in an asymptomatic patient with fibroids; there is no evidence for that indication.
Uterine artery embolization is not advised for patients who desire future fertility because of possible decreased fertility, higher miscarriage risk, and adverse pregnancy outcomes.

evidence_boundaries.statement: Treatment is not determined by the mere presence of a fibroid: distinguish asymptomatic disease from bleeding, bulk, or fertility-related disease, and distinguish uterus-preserving options from definitive hysterectomy.

evidence_notes: The 2025 SOGC guideline was used instead of superseded Guideline No. 318. Fertility claims are limited to the explicit scope and recommendations in No. 461.
